phases.definition: Activities that happen before any real model/data is finalized: requirements, architecture, threat modeling, vendor/tool choices, intended RAG design, agent tool design, identity/auth design.
Anything that targets or depends on the foundation model training corpus, training pipeline, or base weights creation.
Anything that targets or depends on instruction-tuning, RLHF/DPO, safety layers, policies, RAG corpus curation, prompt templates, or agent memory/tool schemas being set up.
Anything that is primarily about testing/benchmarking/red-teaming (internal or external) before release, including attempts to elicit failures in a controlled setting.

Strictly: the act of putting the system into production and integrating it into the real environment: hosting, API gateway, auth, app integration, tool connectors, logging, permissions, secrets, CI/CD release.
Anything that happens after deployment, including: abuse, misuse, drift, jailbreak attempts in the wild, incident detection, telemetry, ongoing discovery, ongoing credential attacks, ongoing evasion.
Any attack whose main lever is: changing what’s running (model version, weights, prompts, policies, RAG index, tools, agent configuration, datasets) or poisoning the update channel.

controls.name: AI-specific threat model before building or adopting
controls.what: Before deciding to build or adopt the system, document its purpose, attack surface and the ATLAS techniques that apply at each phase, with the control chosen for each one and the residual risk accepted by a named owner. Repeat the analysis whenever the configuration, model, tools or data sources change.
controls.evidence: Versioned threat model; risk register with ATLAS technique, assigned control and residual risk; signed acceptance record.

iso.name: Secure system architecture and engineering principles

controls.name: Remove unnecessary capabilities and modalities
controls.what: Disable the model capabilities the purpose does not need (input modalities, tools, code execution, browsing, link output) and justify in writing every capability that stays enabled.
controls.evidence: Inventory of enabled capabilities with justification; configuration showing the disabled ones.

iso.name: Secure system architecture and engineering principles

controls.name: Human oversight designed as a security control
controls.what: Define which decisions or outputs a person reviews, with a real ability to stop, reverse or override the system, and the technical measures that make this possible (interface, alerts, stop button).
controls.evidence: Specification of the oversight points; documented test of stopping and reverting.
controls.appliesWhen: When outputs affect people, money or systems

controls.name: AI threat intelligence programme
controls.what: Continuously follow AI-specific threat sources (security advisories, ATLAS, model and package repositories, sector incidents) and turn relevant findings into updates of the threat model and the controls.
controls.evidence: Subscribed sources; periodic reports; threat model changes traced to an alert.

controls.name: AI bill of materials (AI BOM)
controls.what: Maintain an AI BOM listing models and checkpoints, datasets, packages, inference runtimes, container images, system prompts, connected tools and data sources, providers and versions. Update it with every change and use it to assess the impact of published vulnerabilities.
controls.evidence: AI BOM in a standard format (e.g. CycloneDX or SPDX) generated in the pipeline; version history.

atlasMitigations.name: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials

iso.name: Inventory of information and other associated assets

controls.name: Dataset provenance
controls.what: Record for each dataset its origin (URL or supplier), date obtained, licence, transformations and versions, so that you can tell whether a published poisoning incident affects the data used.
controls.evidence: Provenance record per dataset; data versioning (hash per version).
controls.appliesWhen: The organisation trains or fine-tunes models, or indexes a RAG corpus

iso.name: Inventory of information and other associated assets

legal.condition: High-risk AI system trained with data

controls.name: Change control for system prompts and agent configuration
controls.what: Version system prompts, templates, guardrail policies and agent configuration; require review and approval before production; record who changed what and when; alert on changes made outside the approved workflow.
controls.evidence: Repository with approved change history; alerts on unauthorised changes.

controls.name: Security documentation of the model for whoever deploys it
controls.what: Give system operators the information relevant to security: training and fine-tuning data sources, scope and limitations, guardrails, known failure modes, retention and recommended review frequency.
controls.evidence: Versioned model security sheet delivered to operators.
controls.appliesWhen: The organisation develops or adapts the model for others

controls.name: Due diligence on AI suppliers and components
controls.what: Before contracting an external model, service, dataset or tool, assess its AI-specific risks, require contractual security commitments (incident notification, updates, conformity with ETSI EN 304 223) and review them periodically.
controls.evidence: Supplier security questionnaire; contract clauses; annual review.
controls.appliesWhen: Uses third-party models, services or artefacts

iso.name: Addressing information security within supplier agreements
Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
Information security for use of cloud services

legal.condition: Provider processing personal data on the organisation's behalf

controls.name: Verify integrity and authenticity of artefacts before loading them
controls.what: Compare the hash of weights, checkpoints, datasets, tokenizers, prompt templates and agent configurations with the value published by an authenticated publisher, and verify signatures where they exist, before importing, loading or deploying. Block loading if they do not match.
controls.evidence: Hash or signature verification log per artefact in the pipeline; deployments blocked because of mismatches.

iso.name: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
Installation of software on operational systems

controls.name: Sign code and components; run only signed ones
controls.what: Cryptographically sign your own code, models and AI BOM components, and configure environments so they only run or load components with a valid signature.
controls.evidence: Signing policy; mandatory verification settings; signature log.

iso.name: Installation of software on operational systems

controls.name: Safe serialisation formats and restricted library loading
controls.what: Do not deserialise formats that can execute code (e.g. pickle) from untrusted sources; use formats without execution (e.g. safetensors) and restrict library loading mechanisms in the environments where models are loaded.
controls.evidence: Policy of allowed formats; pipeline check that rejects disallowed formats.

iso.name: Installation of software on operational systems

controls.name: Scanning of artefacts and dependencies
controls.what: Scan models, containers and packages for malicious code, unsafe calls and known vulnerabilities before using them; the scanner must treat corrupt or malformed model files as suspicious, not as safe.
controls.evidence: Scan reports in the pipeline; approved exceptions.

controls.name: Justification and compensating controls for poorly documented components
controls.what: If a model or component lacks sufficient documentation or security assurances, document why it is used, assess its risk, apply compensating controls and tell users in an accessible way.
controls.evidence: Documented justification; risk assessment; communication to users.

iso.name: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain

controls.name: Re-evaluate third-party models before use and at every new version
controls.what: Re-run your own functional and security evaluations on any model published by third parties before using it and whenever its version changes, including tests for backdoors and anomalous behaviour.
controls.evidence: Evaluation report per model version; acceptance criteria.

iso.name: Security testing in development and acceptance

controls.name: Sanitisation and quarantine of training and fine-tuning data
controls.what: Before training or fine-tuning, inspect samples, labels and metadata (inconsistent labels, anomalous samples, distribution shifts, duplicates or repeated patterns) and quarantine anything suspicious. Repeat for every new batch of data.
controls.evidence: Validation report per data batch; quarantine log and decisions.
controls.appliesWhen: The organisation trains or fine-tunes models

legal.condition: High-risk AI system trained with data

controls.name: Restricted access to training data and model registries
controls.what: Limit reading and writing of datasets, model registries and artefact stores to approved identities, with separate permissions to read and to publish; review access periodically.
controls.evidence: Permission matrix; periodic access review; access logs.
controls.appliesWhen: Whenever own data or models are stored

atlasMitigations.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest

controls.name: Separate environments for development, fine-tuning and production
controls.what: Keep dedicated, technically separated environments for development, training and production, with least privilege; non-public training data exists only in the training and development environments.
controls.evidence: Environment diagram; network and permission rules; proof that production cannot access training data.
controls.appliesWhen: The organisation trains or fine-tunes models

iso.name: Separation of development, test and production environments

controls.name: Control of continuous learning from user data
controls.what: User data and feedback are never added to training automatically: they go through sanitisation (DAT-01), per-user contribution thresholds, validation of the resulting model (TST-01) and the ability to roll back to the previous version.
controls.evidence: Documented intake workflow; metrics before and after; tested rollback procedure.
controls.appliesWhen: Learns from user data or is retrained continuously

legal.condition: High-risk AI system that continues to learn after being put into service

controls.name: Secure RAG ingestion
controls.what: Index only authorised sources; inspect content at ingestion and at retrieval for malicious instructions, deceptive claims or content that imitates other results; keep the provenance of each chunk and quarantine suspicious content before indexing.
controls.evidence: List of authorised sources; ingestion log with provenance; quarantine log.
controls.appliesWhen: Uses RAG or ingests external content

controls.name: Permission filter before retrieval and redaction of secrets
controls.what: Apply the requesting user's permissions before retrieval (not after the model has read the document); detect and redact credentials and secrets in retrieved documents before they enter the context or are returned.
controls.evidence: Isolation tests between users or clients; redaction logs.

atlasMitigations.name: Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools

controls.name: Privacy-preserving training and inference
controls.what: When the model is trained with sensitive data, apply mechanisms such as differential privacy, federated training or confidential computing, and measure the residual risk of membership inference and extraction of memorised data.
controls.evidence: Mechanism configuration (e.g. privacy budget); inference test report.
controls.appliesWhen: Trains with personal or confidential data

controls.name: Minimisation and pseudonymisation of training data
controls.what: Remove unnecessary attributes, pseudonymise direct identifiers and generalise values before training or indexing, to reduce what an inference or extraction attack could reveal.
controls.evidence: Specification of transformations per dataset; check that no direct identifiers remain.
controls.appliesWhen: Trains or indexes with personal data

controls.name: Hardening against adversarial examples
controls.what: Train the predictive model to keep its performance on digitally or physically perturbed inputs (adversarial training, robust architectures, certified robustness) and measure degradation with adaptive attacks.
controls.evidence: Clean and under-attack accuracy metrics; perturbation parameters evaluated.

controls.name: Diverse model ensembles
controls.what: Combine models with different architectures, data or training procedures, using an aggregation rule that prevents an input that fools one model from controlling the final prediction.
controls.evidence: Description of the ensemble and aggregation rule; attack transfer tests.

controls.name: Input restoration before inference
controls.what: Preprocess inputs to remove or reduce adversarial perturbations (denoising, compression, resampling, randomised transformations), evaluated against attackers who know the preprocessing.
controls.evidence: Preprocessing specification; results against adaptive attacks.

controls.name: Adversarial input detection
controls.what: Detect and block adversarial examples before inference and watch for query patterns typical of generating them (black-box optimisation, transfer).
controls.evidence: Deployed detector and its metrics; logged alerts and blocks.

controls.name: Fusion of independent sensors
controls.what: Do not rely on a single sensor: corroborate observations across sensors of different modalities or viewpoints so that manipulating one does not determine the prediction.
controls.evidence: Sensor architecture; tests with one sensor manipulated or obstructed.

controls.name: Synthetic content detection on untrusted inputs
controls.what: Apply deepfake detection to images, audio or video supplied by users, especially for identity verification, and block or escalate suspicious content for review.
controls.evidence: Deployed detector; detection rate in tests; escalation workflow.
controls.appliesWhen: Identity verification or decisions based on third-party image, audio or video

controls.name: Safety alignment of the generative model
controls.what: Fine-tune the generative model (e.g. supervised or preference-based fine-tuning) to refuse harmful instructions and out-of-policy actions, and evaluate the result with attack cases.
controls.evidence: Alignment data and criteria; evaluation results before and after.
controls.appliesWhen: The organisation fine-tunes a generative model

controls.name: Mandatory authentication and identity verification on AI endpoints
controls.what: Require authentication on every inference and configuration endpoint, verify identity before granting access to new accounts, protect sessions and monitor use to detect abuse of valid credentials, cookies or replayed tokens.
controls.evidence: Authentication configuration; onboarding process; anomalous use alerts.
controls.appliesWhen: API or interface accessible to users

atlasMitigations.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production

controls.name: Rate, burst and quota limits per identity
controls.what: Limit requests per user, API key, client or device, combining rate, burst and concurrency limits with long-term quotas, and watch for attempts to evade them by spreading requests across accounts.
controls.evidence: Limit configuration; evasion alerts; load tests.

atlasMitigations.name: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate

controls.name: Resource consumption limits per request and per workflow
controls.what: Set limits on input size, context and output tokens, time, memory and compute per request; for agents, limits on iterations, retries, tool calls, delegation and spending.
controls.evidence: Limit configuration; alerts on anomalous consumption.

controls.name: Protect stored system prompts and configurations
controls.what: Restrict access to system prompts, templates, tool definitions and configurations; authenticate and log access to configuration interfaces. The system prompt must not contain secrets.
controls.evidence: Permissions on the configuration store; access logs.

atlasMitigations.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest
Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production

controls.name: Management of the AI system's secrets and credentials
controls.what: No credentials in prompts, agent configurations, code, unprotected environment variables or indexed corpora: use a secrets manager, short-lived and minimally scoped credentials, rotation and exposed-secret detection.
controls.evidence: Inventory of the system's credentials; secret scanning with no findings; rotation policy.
controls.appliesWhen: The system uses credentials for tools, data or services

controls.name: Encryption of models and sensitive data
controls.what: Encrypt models, datasets and sensitive data at rest and in transit, with key management separated from the data.
controls.evidence: Encryption configuration; key management policy.

controls.name: Least privilege of the AI system on other systems
controls.what: The service accounts and permissions the AI system holds on other systems and data sources are limited to what its function requires and are assessed before being granted.
controls.evidence: Inventory of the system's permissions with justification; periodic review.
controls.appliesWhen: The system connects to other systems or data

controls.name: Vulnerability and patch management
controls.what: Apply security updates and patches to the model, its dependencies and its infrastructure; if updating is not possible, apply contingency mitigations; inform whoever deploys the system of relevant updates.
controls.evidence: Vulnerability register and remediation deadlines; update notices issued.

controls.name: Security testing of the exposed application and API
controls.what: In addition to AI-specific testing, subject the application and API that expose the model to classic vulnerability scanning and penetration testing before deployment and periodically.
controls.evidence: Test reports; findings tracked to closure.

iso.name: Security testing in development and acceptance

controls.name: Limit public information about the AI stack and the organisation
controls.what: Review articles, job offers, documentation, application metadata and team profiles before publication so they do not reveal architecture, models, datasets, agent tools or the identities of key people.
controls.evidence: Pre-publication review procedure; review log.

controls.name: Limit publication of model artefacts
controls.what: Do not publish data, algorithms, architectures or checkpoints used in production, or representative of them, except by documented decision.
controls.evidence: Artefact publication policy; inventory of what has been published.

controls.name: Reduce the information returned by predictive inference
controls.what: Return only what the application needs: no confidence scores, logits, rankings, embeddings or model metadata unless justified, and with reduced precision when they are needed.
controls.evidence: API response specification; review of what is exposed.

controls.name: Serve the model from the cloud instead of distributing it
controls.what: Wherever feasible, serve the model and compute features in a controlled environment instead of distributing the weights to the user's device; if they are distributed, apply encryption and binary protection.
controls.evidence: Documented architecture decision; protections applied if distributed.

controls.name: Check that outputs do not allow reconstructing the model or the data
controls.what: Before releasing the system, verify that its outputs do not allow inferring non-public aspects of the model or the training data, or give users unintended influence over the system.
controls.evidence: Report of extraction, inversion and membership inference tests.

controls.name: Injection and jailbreak detection on user inputs
controls.what: Evaluate every prompt and the conversation history for attempts to override instructions or bypass restrictions, without resetting restrictions just because a new turn starts, and block or send to review anything suspicious.
controls.evidence: Deployed input guardrail; detection metrics; block log.

controls.name: Treat all external content as untrusted
controls.what: Separate instructions from data: web content, documents, emails, links that prefill a query and tool responses are marked with their provenance and inspected for instructions before entering the context; they are never treated as a user command.
controls.evidence: Context template design that delimits sources; guardrail on external content.

atlasMitigations.name: Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components

controls.name: Normalisation and detection of hidden instructions
controls.what: Normalise and decode supported representations (Unicode, encodings, hidden formatting) and inspect images, audio, video and metadata for hidden instructions or triggers before ingestion.
controls.evidence: Normalisation rules; tests with obfuscated and multimodal payloads.

controls.name: Output filtering: system instructions, memorised data and sensitive data
controls.what: Inspect every response before delivery to block or redact system instructions, internal information, other users' history or memory, memorised personal or confidential data and reproduced malicious payloads.
controls.evidence: Deployed output guardrail; leakage tests; redaction log.

controls.name: Versioned behavioural guidelines
controls.what: Define behavioural policies in the system prompt and templates (what not to reveal, what not to execute, how to treat external content). They are a defence layer, not a security boundary: combine them with GEN-01 to GEN-04 and AGT-03.
controls.evidence: Versioned system prompt and policies (INV-03); compliance tests.

controls.name: Safe rendering of responses
controls.what: Validate generated HTML, Markdown, links and embedded resources before rendering them; block unauthorised destinations and the automatic loading of remote images or resources that could encode data in the URL.
controls.evidence: Interface content policy; exfiltration tests via links and images.

controls.name: Verification of generated citations and entities
controls.what: Check generated package names, commands, URLs, addresses and citations against authoritative sources before presenting them as valid or using them; flag or suppress unverified ones.
controls.evidence: List of authoritative sources; verification log; tests with invented entities.
controls.appliesWhen: Generates code, packages, links or citations

controls.name: Blocking of generated malicious commands and code
controls.what: Inspect requests and the generated commands or code against the task context and the service policy, and block the generation or delivery of malicious commands.
controls.evidence: Policy rules; tests with malicious requests.

controls.name: Integrity of conversation history
controls.what: Store history on the server, not editable by the client, with a change log and integrity protection; never accept history reconstructed by the client as the source of truth.
controls.evidence: History storage design; tampering test from the client.
controls.appliesWhen: Keeps history across turns or sessions
controls.noSourceWhy: No source prescribes protecting conversation history; it matters because ATLAS documents its manipulation (AML.T0092) to hide the attacker's actions.

controls.name: Least privilege for service agents
controls.what: Limit agents with their own identity to explicitly authorised workflows, with minimally scoped identities, credentials, tools and resources.
controls.evidence: Inventory of agents with permissions and authorised workflows.

controls.name: Least privilege for agents acting on behalf of a user
controls.what: Bind the agent's identity to the user who authorises it; the agent receives only the permissions the task needs, never all of the user's permissions.
controls.evidence: Delegation design; test showing the agent does not inherit unnecessary permissions.

controls.name: Access control enforced in the tool, outside the model
controls.what: Authenticate the caller and authorise each operation in the tool itself, MCP server, gateway or underlying service; the tool's privileges never expand the caller's.
controls.evidence: Authorisation configuration in each tool; escalation tests across users or clients.

atlasMitigations.name: Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools

controls.name: Human approval of impactful actions
controls.what: Require a person's approval before the agent performs write, delete, payment, external sending or configuration change actions, according to a prior classification of each action's impact.
controls.evidence: Classification of actions by impact; log of approvals and rejections.
controls.appliesWhen: Agents with write or execution tools

atlasMitigations.name: Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions

controls.name: Restrict tools when untrusted content enters
controls.what: When untrusted content enters the context, block automatic tool invocation or require user confirmation, in proportion to the severity of the action.
controls.evidence: Restriction rule based on context provenance; tests with indirect injection.

atlasMitigations.name: Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data

controls.name: Validation of tool calls and their inputs and outputs
controls.what: Validate tool, arguments, destinations and data against the authorised task before execution; apply schema checks, sensitive data detection and sanitisation to what goes in and out of each tool, outside the model.
controls.evidence: Validation schemas and rules; log of blocked calls.

atlasMitigations.name: Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components

controls.name: Hardening of persistent memory
controls.what: Control how the agent's memory is created, modified, isolated, audited and recovered: inspect every write and read, separate by user, log changes and allow returning to a clean state.
controls.evidence: Memory design with per-user isolation; write log; cleanup procedure.

controls.name: Isolation of agent execution
controls.what: Run the agent's tools and code in ephemeral containers or virtual machines built from clean images, with restricted network and file system and no state carried between runs.
controls.evidence: Isolated environment configuration; escape tests.
controls.appliesWhen: Agents with code execution or tools

controls.name: Prevent autonomous expansion of authority
controls.what: Set the agent's maximum authority before execution; resources, identities or destinations discovered during execution stay out of scope until validated. The control is enforced outside the agent.
controls.evidence: Definition of the authorised scope; logged blocks.

controls.name: Detection of agent goal drift
controls.what: Continuously evaluate whether the planned actions remain consistent with the authorised goal, and stop or escalate when they deviate.
controls.evidence: Consistency rule or evaluator; logged alerts and stops.

controls.name: Lifecycle of resources created by agents
controls.what: Treat the identities, compute, storage and other resources an agent creates or obtains as attributable assets: inventory them, assign an owner and an expiry, and delete them when finished.
controls.evidence: Inventory of agent-created resources; logged deletions.

atlasMitigations.name: AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management

controls.name: Review third-party tools before exposing them to the model
controls.what: Review the descriptions, schemas, examples and instructions of every third-party tool or MCP server before connecting it; reject those containing instructions unrelated to their function, and pin the reviewed version.
controls.evidence: Review log per tool and version; list of approved tools.

controls.name: Agent configuration protected against modification
controls.what: The agent's configuration (prompt, tools, triggers, shared memory) cannot be modified by the agent itself or by users; changes go through INV-03 and changes outside that workflow are detected.
controls.evidence: Read-only permissions at runtime; change alerts.
controls.noSourceWhy: No source prescribes locking the agent configuration; it matters because ATLAS documents its modification (AML.T0081) and discovery (AML.T0084).

controls.name: Functional and security validation before deployment and after every change
controls.what: Evaluate the model with representative data and adversarial cases before deployment and after every fine-tuning, update or change of context, including tests for poisoning, tampering and backdoors.
controls.evidence: Evaluation plan and results per version; signed acceptance criteria.

iso.name: Security testing in development and acceptance

controls.name: Independent and recurring AI red team
controls.what: Run authorised red team exercises based on the identified threats, on the complete system (model, data, tools, integrations), before deployment and periodically, with independent testers and follow-up of findings.
controls.evidence: Scope, report and remediation plan for each exercise.
controls.appliesWhen: Always; in practice essential for exposed or high-impact systems

iso.name: Security testing in development and acceptance

legal.condition: General-purpose AI model with systemic risk (provider)

controls.name: AI security telemetry
controls.what: Log access, changes and operations across the lifecycle: requests and responses, model and data versions, tool calls, access to model registries and data; with enough context to correlate activity across accounts and components, and protected against deletion or tampering.
controls.evidence: Logging schema; defined retention; detection use cases in the SIEM.

controls.name: Monitoring of model behaviour and drift
controls.what: Monitor the model's performance and behaviour in production to detect sudden or gradual changes that may indicate poisoning, tampering or drift, with defined thresholds and response.
controls.evidence: Metrics and thresholds; logged alerts and investigations.

controls.name: Detection of extraction and adaptive response degradation
controls.what: Detect patterns of extraction, distillation or inference about training data and, depending on confidence and severity, degrade responses to that activity in a targeted way while preserving legitimate use.
controls.evidence: Detection rules; log of degradations applied.

controls.name: AI decoys
controls.what: Deploy decoy AI services, agents or credentials with no real function and monitor them: any interaction is a reliable sign of reconnaissance or unauthorised access.
controls.evidence: Inventory of decoys; alerts generated.

controls.name: Detection of internal environment reconnaissance
controls.what: Monitor enumeration of accounts, cloud resources, information repositories and environment configuration from the AI system's identities and runs, and alert on discovery patterns.
controls.evidence: Detection use cases; investigated alerts.
controls.appliesWhen: The system has access to the network or internal resources
controls.noSourceWhy: No AI source prescribes this detection; it matters because ATLAS documents environment discovery (AML.T0075, AML.T0089) with no associated mitigation.

controls.name: AI-specific incident response and recovery plan
controls.what: Maintain and test an incident plan and a recovery plan covering AI-specific attacks (poisoning, extraction, injection, agent abuse), able to return to a known good state of model, data, index and configuration, and to support users and affected parties.
controls.evidence: Approved plans; exercises carried out; restorable copies of models and indexes.

iso.name: Information security incident management planning and preparation

legal.condition: General-purpose AI model with systemic risk (provider)

controls.name: Public vulnerability disclosure policy
controls.what: Publish a clear and accessible policy so that third parties can report vulnerabilities in the AI system, with a channel and response times.
controls.evidence: Published policy; log of reports received.

controls.name: Role-based AI security training
controls.what: Include AI security content in training, tailored to each role and updated when new threats appear; specific training for developers in secure AI coding and supply chain risks (malicious artefacts).
controls.evidence: Training plan per role; attendance and assessment.

iso.name: Information security awareness, education and training

legal.condition: Providers and deployers of any AI system

controls.name: User awareness of deepfakes and AI-generated phishing
controls.what: Train users and exposed staff to recognise impersonation with synthetic content and AI-generated phishing, with a channel to report them.
controls.evidence: Campaigns and simulations; reporting rate.

iso.name: Information security awareness, education and training

controls.name: Security information for users
controls.what: Inform users in an accessible way about how their data is used and stored, appropriate use of the system, its limitations and failure modes, unresolved threats and planned security or model updates.
controls.evidence: Published usage guide; update notices issued.

controls.name: Secure deletion when retiring or transferring models and data
controls.what: When retiring or transferring a model, dataset or system, securely delete data, weights, indexes, memories and configurations, involving whoever is custodian of the data.
controls.evidence: Deletion record; supplier certificate where applicable.

notes: No mitigation in ATLAS 2026.10: covered only by proposed controls

jnic.description:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's identity that can be used during targeting. Information about identities may include a variety of details, including personal data (ex: employee names, email addresses, photos, etc.) as well as sensitive details such as credentials or multi-factor authentication (MFA) configurations.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct elicitation, Search Victim-Owned Websites, or via leaked information on the black market.

Adversaries may use the gathered victim data to Create Deepfakes and impersonate them in a convincing manner. This may create opportunities for adversaries to Establish Accounts under the impersonated identity, or allow them to perform convincing Phishing attacks.
jnic.whyAiAct: This mitigation should arguably not be directly mandated in the AI Act, because it primarily concerns organisational identity management, users' information expousure and human verification procedures that lie outside the AI system itself. The attack vector exploits weaknesses in account governance, credential practices, and social engineering resilience rather than flaws intrinsic to the AI model’s design or operation. As such, these controls fall more appropriately within regulation such as DSA or DMA rather than product-level AI regulation.

jnic.description:
Adversaries may search open application repositories during targeting. Examples of these include Google Play, the iOS App store, the macOS App Store, and the Microsoft Store.

Adversaries may craft search queries seeking applications that contain AI-enabled components. Frequently, the next step is to Acquire Public AI Artifacts.
jnic.coverage:
There is no article or recital in the AI Act that requires organisations to:

- restrict public disclosure of AI architectures, techniques, datasets, or model design, or

- limit disclosure of organisational details (researchers’ names, departments, locations) to prevent adversarial targeting.

Partially, Recitals 64–65 require providers of high-risk AI systems to implement a continuous risk-management system covering reasonably foreseeable misuse, including malicious interactions with the system

jnic.description:
Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting. By utilizing serverless infrastructure, adversaries can make it more difficult to attribute infrastructure used during operations back to them.

Once acquired, the serverless runtime environment can be leveraged to either respond directly to infected machines or to Proxy traffic to an adversary-owned command and control server. As traffic generated by these functions will appear to come from subdomains of common cloud providers, it may be difficult to distinguish from ordinary traffic to these providers. This can be used to bypass a Content Security Policy which prevent retrieving content from arbitrary locations.

jnic.description: Adversaries may develop their own adversarial attacks. They may leverage existing libraries as a starting point (Adversarial AI Attack Implementations). They may implement ideas described in public research papers or develop custom made attacks for the victim model.
jnic.coverage: No direct AI Act control over publishing/obtaining attack libraries (this is attacker-side “resource development”). The only meaningful connection is defensive: providers of high-risk systems must implement cybersecurity measures covering adversarial examples/evasion (Art. 15(5)), continuously manage risks incl. foreseeable misuse (Art. 9), and inform deployers about robustness/cybersecurity levels and foreseeable misuse contexts (Art. 13).
jnic.whyAiAct: This technique is common precisely because open-source attack code exists; the AI Act should not try to suppress legitimate security research. What it should do (and only does implicitly) is require providers to assume the availability of commodity adversarial tooling as part of “reasonably foreseeable misuse” and reflect that assumption in mandatory adversarial evaluation and monitoring evidence. Without that prescriptiveness, two providers can both claim Art. 15(5) compliance yet have very different real-world robustness against “off-the-shelf” attacks.

jnic.description:
Adversaries may search for and obtain generative AI models or tools, such as large language models (LLMs), to assist them in various steps of their operation. Generative AI can be used in a variety of malicious ways, such as to generating malware, to Generate Deepfakes, to Generate Malicious Commands, for Retrieval Content Crafting, or to generate Phishing content.

Adversaries may obtain open source models and serve them locally using frameworks such as Ollama or vLLM. They may host them using cloud infrastructure. Or, they may leverage AI service providers such as HuggingFace.

They may need to jailbreak the model (see LLM Jailbreak) to bypass any restrictions put in place to limit the types of responses it can generate. They may also need to break the terms of service of the model's developer.

Generative AI models may also be "uncensored" meaning they are designed to generate content without any restrictions such as guardrails or content filters. Uncensored GenAI is ripe for abuse by cybercriminals [1] [2]. Models may be fine-tuned to remove alignment and guardrails [3] or be subjected to targeted manipulations to bypass refusal [4] resulting in uncensored variants of the model. Uncensored models may be built for offensive and defensive cybersecurity [5], which can be abused by an adversary. There are also models that are expressly designed and advertised for malicious use [6].
jnic.coverage:
High-risk AI systems: must meet lifecycle robustness/cybersecurity and adversarial-vulnerability coverage (Art. 15)

GPAI models: provider obligations in Art. 53 include technical documentation, downstream info, copyright policy, and public training-content summary; open-source GPAI can be exempt from some documentation duties unless systemic risk (Art. 53(2)).

GPAI with systemic risk: Art. 55 requires state-of-the-art evaluation incl. adversarial testing, systemic-risk mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure

The AI Act addresses this mainly through provider duties (especially Art. 55 for systemic-risk models), but there are structural limits: many malicious uses rely on open-source or non-systemic models and may fall outside the strictest obligations, and the Act does not create a general “misuse-prevention” duty for all GenAI distribution channels. Strong guardrails for all GPAI security by default to all.

Adversaries may discover the ontology of an AI model's output space, for example, the types of objects a model can detect. The adversary may discovery the ontology by repeated queries to the model, forcing it to enumerate its output space. The model ontology helps the adversary understand how the model is being used by the victim. It is useful to the adversary in creating targeted attacks.

There is no article nor recital that prescribes concrete technical measures against this type of attacks. However, at a high level of abstraction and only for high-risk systems. Recitals 64–66 require providers of high-risk AI systems to implement a continuous risk-management system covering reasonably foreseeable misuse, including malicious interaction with the system. Repeated probing to infer a model’s output ontology falls within this category. Similarly, Recital 76 recognises AI-specific cybersecurity threats, including inference-based and adversarial attacks, and requires high-risk AI systems to be protected through suitable measures.

Thus, the AI Act acknowledges the type of risk addressed by ontology-discovery mitigations, but only indirectly, for high-risk systems, and in abstract terms.

jnic.whyAiAct:
This issue should have been explicitly contemplated in the AI Act because the Regulation structurally promotes transparency—through mandatory documentation and disclosure obligations (e.g., Articles 11, 13, Annex IV, and Article 53 for GPAI models)—without equally specifying safeguards to manage the security risks that such transparency may create. In the pre-training phase, publicly accessible or production-representative datasets, architectural descriptions, or technical summaries can significantly lower the barrier for adversarial reconnaissance, enabling tailored data poisoning, adversarial input crafting, or system profiling. The Act treats transparency primarily as a risk-mitigation and accountability tool, but it does not explicitly address the tension between disclosure and attack-surface expansion.
Given that dataset reconnaissance and public data collection are well-documented adversarial techniques, the AI Act could have incorporated clearer governance requirements distinguishing between necessary regulatory transparency and security-sensitive technical exposure. For example, it could have required dataset exposure risk assessments, artefact classification policies (e.g., production-representative vs. research-only data), or operational safeguards to prevent unintended public accessibility. Without such provisions, the Regulation leaves providers to independently balance compliance transparency with adversarial risk, creating a structural blind spot in pre-training security governance.

jnic.description: Adversaries may create an entity they control, such as a software package, website, or email address to a source hallucinated by an LLM. The hallucinations may take the form of package names commands, URLs, company names, or email addresses that point the victim to the entity controlled by the adversary. When the victim interacts with the adversary-controlled entity, the attack can proceed.
jnic.coverage:
There is no article or recital in the AI Act that explicitly requires providers to:
constrain or verify external references (e.g., URLs, package names, emails, organisations) generated by AI systems before presenting them to users, or
design user interfaces to technically reduce the likelihood of follow-through on unverified or uncertain entities.
Partially, Arts. 9, 13 and 15 require high-risk AI systems to implement risk management, ensure appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness, and inform deployers about limitations and foreseeable misuse.
However, the AI Act treats hallucinations primarily as a reliability issue. It does not explicitly recognise that hallucinated entities can become attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., newly registered domains or malicious packages), transforming an accuracy defect into a supply-chain or social-engineering attack vector. Transparency, monitoring and cybersecurity are required at a general level, but the Regulation does not mandate specific safeguards against actionable hallucinated references.
jnic.whyAiAct: This technique is not merely generic inaccuracy; it is a repeatable abuse pattern in which ungrounded outputs become operational pointers that adversaries can deliberately register or control. The AI Act would have been materially stronger if it had included explicit expectations to prevent hallucinated entities from being treated as trustworthy references—for example, requirements to verify or constrain external links and packages before display, to clearly flag unverifiable entities, or to introduce interaction friction when users attempt to act on uncertain outputs. Without such operational guidance, the Regulation relies on high-level validity and monitoring duties that are not sufficient to mitigate this specific and foreseeable exploitation pathway.

jnic.description: Adversaries may Poison Training Data and publish it to a public location. The poisoned dataset may be a novel dataset or a poisoned variant of an existing open source dataset. This data may be introduced to a victim system via AI Supply Chain Compromise.
jnic.coverage:
The AI Act does not apply to phases previous to deployment or production as set in art. 2(8) AI Act "This Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service".

Partially it is included in art. 10(2)(b) AI Act but only for hish risk systems:
" Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate
for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Those practices shall concern in particular: (b) data collection processes and the origin of data, and in the case of personal data, the original purpose of the data collection; "
jnic.whyAiAct: The exclusion in art. 2(8) AI Act creates a structural cybersecurity gap because many of the most consequential AI security failures occur during research, training, fine-tuning, i.e., before a system is placed on the market. By explicitly excluding these phases, the Act regulates the output of development but not the integrity of the development pipeline itself. Although Article 10(2)(b) partially addresses data governance by requiring high-risk systems to document data collection processes and origin, this obligation is limited in scope (only high-risk systems) and focused primarily on data quality and lawfulness rather than integrity or tamper-resistance. It does not mandate technical safeguards such as cryptographic verification of datasets, secure artifact management, dataset provenance chains, or AI Bills of Materials. As a result, the Act leaves the one of the most vulnerable phase of the AI lifecycle—where systemic vulnerabilities can be embedded irreversibly into foundation models—largely unregulated.

notes: No mitigation in ATLAS 2026.10: covered only by proposed controls

jnic.description:
Adversaries may write content designed to be retrieved by user queries and influence a user of the system in some way. This abuses the trust the user has in the system.

The crafted content can be combined with a prompt injection. It can also stand alone in a separate document or email. The adversary must get the crafted content into the victim\u0027s database, such as a vector database used in a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system. This may be accomplished via cyber access, or by abusing the ingestion mechanisms common in RAG systems (see RAG Poisoning).

Large language models may be used as an assistant to aid an adversary in crafting content.
jnic.coverage:
Partially, for high-risk AI systems, only certain provisions of the AI Act can be read as indirectly relevant to Retrieval Content Crafting. The connection is limited and must be interpreted through specific clauses:

Art. 9(2)–(4) Risk management system: requires identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, including those arising from reasonably foreseeable misuse, and testing of mitigation measures. A provider could argue that adversarially crafted retrieval content constitutes foreseeable misuse of the system’s ingestion or retrieval pipeline.

Art. 15(5) Cybersecurity: requires resilience against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter use, outputs, or performance, including prevention, detection, and mitigation of attacks such as data poisoning or adversarial manipulation. Retrieval content crafting could fall within “manipulation” of system outputs via injected content.
The indirect coverage of Retrieval Content Crafting through Arts. 9, 13, 14, 15(5), 72 and 73 is limited strictly to high-risk AI systems.
jnic.whyAiAct: RAG is a dominant pattern where untrusted content is intentionally ingested and surfaced, making retrieval content crafting a predictable and recurrent failure mode rather than an edge case. This attack exploits a concrete trust boundary—retrieved content being implicitly treated as “evidence”—and can steer users through poisoned documents, emails, or web pages injected into the vector database. High-level duties on risk management, cybersecurity, transparency, and monitoring are necessary but not operationally sufficient to drive consistent implementation of RAG-specific controls. The AI Act would have been materially stronger if it had included explicit expectations for securing ingestion paths, segregating trusted/untrusted sources, preventing instruction-like retrieval content from overriding system intent, and requiring measurable validation/monitoring criteria for retrieved content—because otherwise teams can satisfy the Act’s outcomes on paper while still deploying retrieval workflows that remain highly vulnerable in practice.

jnic.description:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed (Develop Capabilities) or obtained (Obtain Capabilities) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary (Acquire Infrastructure) or was otherwise compromised by them. Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub, model registries, such as Hugging Face, or container registries.

Adversaries may stage a variety of AI Artifacts including poisoned datasets (Publish Poisoned Datasets, malicious models (Publish Poisoned Models, and prompt injections. They may target names of legitimate companies or products, engage in typosquatting, or use hallucinated entities (Discover LLM Hallucinations).
jnic.coverage:
Recital (76) acknowledges AI-specific cybersecurity threats, including adversarial manipulation and inference-based attacks, and requires high-risk systems to be protected through suitable technical measures but it does not specify.

Recital (110) ecognizes the importance of cybersecurity to prevent unauthorized access and manipulation. However, it remains high-level and does not prescribe artifact provenance controls. Thus, Stage Capabilities is only indirectly and abstractly covered under general cybersecurity and risk-management duties for high-risk systems. There is no explicit supply-chain integrity obligation tailored to AI artifact staging in the Regulation.
jnic.whyAiAct: Stage Capabilities should at least have been conceptually contemplated in the AI Act because it exploits normal AI development practices (downloading models, datasets, or containers from public registries where adversaries can stage malicious or lookalike artifacts. While some provisions can be interpreted as indirectly covering such supply-chain risks for high-risk systems, they remain abstract and outcome-based. The Act does not explicitly recognise AI artifact provenance and secure intake controls as a distinct cybersecurity concern. Given that supply-chain manipulation is a recognised and repeatable attack pattern, clearer acknowledgment of AI-specific supply-chain integrity expectations would have strengthened the Regulation without turning it into a technical standard.

jnic.description:
Adversaries may target software packages that are commonly used in AI-enabled systems or are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle. This can include deep learning frameworks used to build AI models (e.g. PyTorch, TensorFlow, Jax), generative AI integration frameworks (e.g. LangChain, LangFlow), inference engines, AI DevOps tools, and Model Context Protocol servers, which give AI agents access to tools and data resources. They may also target the dependency chains of any of these software packages [1]. Additionally, adversaries may target specific components used by AI software such as configuration files [2] or example usage of AI tools, which may be distributed in Jupyter notebooks [3].

Adversaries may compromise legitimate packages [4] or publish malicious software to a namesquatted location [1]. They may target package names that are hallucinated by large language models [5] (see: Publish Hallucinated Entities). They may also perform a "rugpull" in which they first publish a legitimate package and then publish a malicious version once they reach a critical mass of users [6].

jnic.whyAiAct: Stage Capabilities should at least have been conceptually contemplated in the AI Act because it exploits normal AI development practices (downloading models, datasets, or containers from public registries where adversaries can stage malicious or lookalike artifacts. While some provisions can be interpreted as indirectly covering such supply-chain risks for high-risk systems, they remain abstract and outcome-based. The Act does not explicitly recognise AI artifact provenance and secure intake controls as a distinct cybersecurity concern. Given that supply-chain manipulation is a recognised and repeatable attack pattern, clearer acknowledgment of AI-specific supply-chain integrity expectations would have strengthened the Regulation without turning it into a technical standard.

jnic.description:
Data is a key vector of supply chain compromise for adversaries. Every AI project will require some form of data. Many rely on large open source datasets that are publicly available. An adversary could rely on compromising these sources of data. The malicious data could be a result of Poison Training Data or include traditional malware.

An adversary can also target private datasets in the labeling phase. The creation of private datasets will often require the hiring of outside labeling services. An adversary can poison a dataset by modifying the labels being generated by the labeling service.
jnic.coverage: The AI Act partially addresses data supply-chain compromise, but only in relation to high-risk AI systems. There is no general, AI-wide obligation mandating dataset integrity or provenance controls across all AI models. For high-risk AI systems, several provisions are relevant: Article 10(2)(b)–(c) requires data governance measures concerning the collection and preparation of training, validation, and testing datasets (including documentation of origin and processing steps such as cleaning and labeling); Article 10(3)–(4) requires assessment of dataset quality (relevance, representativeness, absence of errors); Article 10(2)(f–g) requires bias detection and mitigation; Article 10(5) imposes safeguards for special categories of data; and Article 15(5) requires cybersecurity measures to protect against attacks, including data poisoning. Additionally, Article 9(2)–(4) (risk management system) can be interpreted as requiring identification and mitigation of foreseeable risks such as compromised or poisoned training data.
jnic.whyAiAct: However, these obligations apply only to high-risk AI systems. AI systems that are not classified as high-risk, as well as general-purpose AI models not designated as systemic risk, are not subject to equivalent dataset integrity or provenance requirements.

jnic.description: AI-enabled systems often rely on open sourced models in various ways. Most commonly, the victim organization may be using these models for fine tuning. These models will be downloaded from an external source and then used as the base for the model as it is tuned on a smaller, private dataset. Loading models often requires executing some saved code in the form of a saved model file. These can be compromised with traditional malware, or through some adversarial AI techniques.
jnic.coverage: The AI Act does not explicitly require provenance/integrity controls for externally sourced model artifacts (e.g., signature verification, trusted registries, safe-loading requirements, mandatory backdoor testing before reuse). For high-risk AI systems, it can only be covered indirectly through Art. 9(2)–(4) (risk management and reasonably foreseeable misuse), Art. 15(5) (cybersecurity resilience against manipulation, including attacks such as model poisoning/data poisoning), and organisational duties like Arts. 16–17 (quality management system). If compromise is detected post-deployment, Art. 72 (post-market monitoring) and Art. 73 (serious incident reporting) may be triggered. At recital level, Recitals 64–66 support a lifecycle risk-management reading (foreseeable misuse/malicious interaction), and Recital 76 recognises AI-specific cybersecurity threats and the need for suitable protective measures—both of which can be interpreted to include model supply-chain threats, but only at a high level.
jnic.whyAiAct: Model supply-chain compromise is a recognised and repeatable failure mode in modern AI workflows, especially because “download-and-load” reuse of external models is normal practice and because compromise can occur without classic endpoint intrusion (e.g., malicious checkpoint, backdoored weights, unsafe serialization). Given the AI Act already relies on cybersecurity and lifecycle risk-management as core pillars for high-risk systems, it would have been reasonable to expect explicit baseline expectations for model artifact authenticity and safe handling (e.g., integrity/provenance verification, secure loading constraints, and backdoor/trigger testing before adoption). Without that specificity, providers can plausibly claim compliance with Arts. 9 and 15(5) while still importing external models in ways that leave the most common compromise pathways largely unmitigated.

jnic.description:
An adversary may compromise a victim's container registry by pushing a manipulated container image and overwriting an existing container name and/or tag. Users of the container registry as well as automated CI/CD pipelines may pull the adversary's container image, compromising their AI Supply Chain. This can affect development and deployment environments.

Container images may include AI models, so the compromised image could have an AI model which was manipulated by the adversary (See Manipulate AI Model).
jnic.coverage:
The AI Act does not contain any provision that explicitly addresses container registry compromise or CI/CD pipeline integrity for AI artifacts. However, for high-risk AI systems, several provisions indirectly touch the issue. Article 15(1) and (5) require high-risk systems to ensure an appropriate level of cybersecurity and resilience against third-party manipulation, including attacks affecting system integrity. Article 17 (quality management system) requires documented procedures covering design control, development, testing, risk management, and post-market monitoring, which may encompass supply-chain security practices. Annex IV (Art. 11) requires documentation of architecture, integration with third-party components, version control, and cybersecurity measures. Additionally, Article 9 (risk management) requires identification and mitigation of foreseeable risks throughout the lifecycle, which could include compromised container images.
However, these obligations apply only to high-risk AI systems. There is no AI-wide obligation requiring integrity verification of container artifacts, registry protection mechanisms, secure tagging practices, CI/CD pull verification, or cryptographic provenance validation. General-purpose AI models (unless systemic risk under Art. 55(1)(d)) and non-high-risk AI systems are not subject to comparable requirements.
jnic.whyAiAct:
Container registry compromise is not an AI-specific vulnerability in a narrow sense; it is a well-known software supply-chain failure mode. However, AI systems amplify its impact because models, weights, dependencies, and inference logic are frequently packaged and distributed as containers. A poisoned image can silently substitute a model, embed backdoors, or alter runtime behavior, directly undermining integrity and potentially affecting safety, fundamental rights, or systemic stability.

It should not necessarily have mandated container-specific controls in detail, but it would have been beneficial for the AI Act (in a recital or clarification) to explicitly recognize AI software supply-chain integrity as part of the cybersecurity obligations. This would reduce interpretive ambiguity while preserving technological neutrality.

notes: Appears 2 times in the matrix

jnic.description:
Adversaries may directly modify an AI model's architecture to re-define it's behavior. This can include adding or removing layers as well as adding pre or post-processing operations.

The effects could include removing the ability to predict certain classes, adding erroneous operations to increase computation costs, or degrading performance. Additionally, a separate adversary-defined network could be injected into the computation graph, which can change the behavior based on the inputs, effectively creating a backdoor.
jnic.coverage:
For high-risk systems, Article 15(5) requires that systems be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs, or functioning. A malicious modification of the model architecture (e.g., adding layers, injecting backdoor sub-networks, modifying computation graphs) constitutes a direct alteration of functioning and therefore falls within this obligation. Recital 77 further clarifies that cybersecurity includes protection against attacks that may manipulate system behaviour.
Additionally, Article 9 (risk management) requires providers to identify and mitigate reasonably foreseeable risks throughout the lifecycle, which logically includes architecture tampering in development, deployment, or supply-chain contexts.
Article 11 and Annex IV require detailed technical documentation of the system architecture, components, and version history. Substantial architecture changes should therefore be traceable. Under Article 43(4), a substantial modification requires a renewed conformity assessment, which would likely apply to architectural alterations.
For GPAI models with systemic risk, Article 55(1)(d) requires ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its infrastructure, which includes integrity of model artifacts.
However, these provisions remain high-level and outcome-based rather than technically prescriptive.
jnic.whyAiAct:
Architecture integrity is a baseline cybersecurity property, not a risk-category feature. Any AI system—regardless of whether it falls under Annex III—can be modified to introduce backdoors, degrade performance, leak data, or embed malicious logic.

Many “non-high-risk” systems are widely deployed general-purpose or embedded components that integrate into larger socio-technical infrastructures. A compromised architecture in a low-risk standalone system can become a supply-chain vector when reused downstream.

Third, the distinction creates a regulatory asymmetry: high-risk systems must implement resilience measures under Article 15, whereas other systems may operate without equivalent integrity safeguards—even if technically identical.

For these reasons, architecture integrity could reasonably be framed as a minimum horizontal cybersecurity obligation applicable to all AI systems, with proportionality scaling the depth of controls.

jnic.description: Adversaries may embed malicious code into AI Model files. AI models may be packaged as a combination of instructions and weights. Some formats such as pickle files are unsafe to deserialize because they can contain unsafe calls such as exec. Models with embedded malware may still operate as expected. It may allow them to achieve Execution, Command & Control, or Exfiltrate Data.

This allows the adversary to embed vulnerabilities in AI models trained on the data that may not be easily detectable. Data poisoning attacks may or may not require modifying the labels. The embedded vulnerability is activated at a later time by data samples with an Insert Backdoor Trigger

Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems and configuration files or local databases, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

This can include basic fingerprinting information and sensitive data such as ssh keys.

jnic.description: The adversary may add a perceptual trigger into inference data. The trigger may be imperceptible or non-obvious to humans. This technique is used in conjunction with Poison AI Model and allows the adversary to produce their desired effect in the target model.

jnic.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an AI model's weights to change it's behavior or performance, resulting in a poisoned model. Adversaries may poison a model by directly manipulating its weights, training the model on poisoned data, further fine-tuning the model, or otherwise interfering with its training process.

The change in behavior of poisoned models may be limited to targeted categories in predictive AI models, or targeted topics, concepts, or facts in generative AI models, or aim for a general performance degradation.
